title: Earth, Moon and Sun
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Earth, Moon and Sun Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how Earth's rotation and revolution cause day, night and years; explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes seasons; describe the phases of the Moon, eclipses and tides. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand E: Earth and Space Systems – Space)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 science worksheets on day and night, seasons, phases of the Moon, eclipses and tides. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Rotation makes day; tilt makes seasons.
key_sub: Earth spins once a day and orbits once a year; the Moon's phases repeat about every month.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours and revolves around the Sun once a year.

  • Day and night come from rotation. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis.
  • The Moon orbits Earth about once a month, and we see different phases of its sunlit half.
  • Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow covers the Moon.
Example

What causes seasons?

tilt toward the Sun in summer

tilt away in winter

Answer: the tilt of Earth's axis

Example

What causes day and night?

Earth spins

Answer: rotation

Common mistakes

  • Thinking seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.
  • Thinking Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases.
  • Mixing up rotation and revolution.

faq.q: What is the difference between rotation and revolution?
faq.a: Rotation is spinning on an axis (one day). Revolution is travelling around the Sun (one year).
Earth's axis is tilted. When our hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight is more direct and days are longer, so it is summer.

faq.q: Why does the Moon have phases?
faq.a: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of the half that the Sun lights up.

items.q: What causes day and night?
items.e: One rotation takes about 24 hours.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to go through all its phases?
items.e: The word month comes from Moon.

items.q: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
items.e: That is why we have years.

items.q: The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 90°?
The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 240°?
Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 6 hours?
At midday in Ontario, where is the Sun?
c: at its highest, in the south
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: Which way does the Earth spin?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Benjamin watches a star for 8 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 105°?
The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, which is 15° every hour. How far does it turn in 5 hours?
What causes ocean tides?
c: mainly the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's water
items.e: Two high tides a day happen in most places.

items.q: Stars seem to move about 15° across the sky each hour because Earth spins. Emma watches a star for 2 hours. About how many degrees does it move?
The Earth turns 15° every hour. How long does it take to turn 165°?
The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, which is 15° every hour. How far does it turn in 3 hours?
What happens in a solar eclipse?
c: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun.
items.e: Never look at the Sun, even during an eclipse.

items.q: Why are shadows shortest at noon?
c: It is always cloudy at noon.
The Sun is lowest in the sky.
The Sun is highest in the sky.
items.e: High Sun, short shadow.

items.q: At sunrise in Ontario, where is the Sun in the sky?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: At sunset in Ontario, where is the Sun?
items.e: Day and night happen because the Earth spins; the Sun only seems to move.

items.q: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in 18 hours?
How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Why do we have seasons?
c: The Sun gets hotter in summer.
The Earth's axis is tilted, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year.
The Moon blocks the Sun in winter.
The Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer.
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: What causes the seasons on Earth?
c: the Earth's changing distance from the Sun
the tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: It is March. Maya lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: Why do we see the same side of the Moon all the time?
c: The Moon spins once for each orbit of Earth.
The other side is dark forever.
items.e: This is called being tidally locked.

items.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
c: the force of gravity between them
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: It is September. Hana lives in the Northern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: It is December. How high is the noon Sun in the sky where Jayden lives in the Northern Hemisphere, compared with the rest of the year?
c: exactly overhead every day of the year
higher than at any other time of year
lower than at any other time of year
items.e: The tilt toward the Sun makes the noon Sun higher in summer and lower in winter.

items.q: Which direction does the Sun appear to rise?
items.e: Earth spins from west to east.

items.q: Why is it warmer in summer?
c: The Sun gives out more energy.
The Earth is much closer to the Sun.
The Sun is higher in the sky, so its energy is more concentrated and days are longer.
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
c: Earth's shadow covers part of it every night.
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
items.e: These are the phases of the Moon.

items.q: Why are winter days short in Ontario?
c: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun.
Clouds block the Sun all day.
items.e: Less daylight and less direct sunlight.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: the tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the Sun
Earth getting closer to the Sun in summer
items.e: In June the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

items.q: It is December. How high is the noon Sun in the sky where Emma lives in the Southern Hemisphere, compared with the rest of the year?
c: higher than at any other time of year
lower than at any other time of year
exactly overhead every day of the year
items.e: The tilt toward the Sun makes the noon Sun higher in summer and lower in winter.

items.q: At about what angle is the Earth's axis tilted?
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Why are days longer in summer in Ontario?
c: The Earth is closer to the Sun.
The Earth spins slower in summer.
The northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun.
The Sun is bigger in summer.
items.e: The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5°.

items.q: It is June. Compared with March, how long are the days where Ethan lives in the Northern Hemisphere?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has longer days.

items.q: Why are days longer in summer in Ontario?
c: The northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun is up for longer.
The Sun is bigger in summer.
The Earth spins slower in summer.
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: What causes day and night?
c: the Sun moving around the Earth
the Earth spinning on its axis once every 24 hours
the Earth orbiting the Sun once a year
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: It is September. Nathan lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: Tonight Kai sees a waning gibbous. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Hana sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning gibbous?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Mateo sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: New: no lit side visible. Full: the whole face is lit.

items.q: Tonight Maya sees a waxing crescent. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the last quarter?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Mei sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning crescent?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Ethan sees a full moon. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Leah sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Tonight Zoe sees a waning crescent. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Liam sees a waxing gibbous. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the new moon?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the new moon?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: What does a sundial use to tell time?
c: the shadow made by the Sun
items.e: Shadows move as Earth rotates.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the first quarter?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Maya sees a waning crescent. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Chloe sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Noah reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
c: the 23.5° tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
items.e: Tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

items.q: About how long does one cycle of Moon phases take?
items.e: About one month.

items.q: Chloe reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Ava photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon.

items.q: Chloe reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Noah photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with new moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous.

items.q: Emma photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → third quarter → new moon → first quarter.

items.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
c: The Sun is too far away.
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon usually do not line up exactly.
items.e: They need a near-perfect line-up.

items.q: Noah reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Emma photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent.

items.q: Lucas photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → new moon → first quarter → full moon.

items.q: Noah reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Noah photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning gibbous → waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous.

items.q: Ethan reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Olivia photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → waning gibbous.

items.q: Is the far side of the Moon always dark?
c: No. It gets sunlight too; we just never see it from Earth.
items.e: It is fully lit at new moon.

items.q: Zoe reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Why is it summer in Ontario in July?
c: Earth is closest to the Sun in July.
The Moon is full in July.
The Sun is hotter in July.
The Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight is more direct and days are longer.
items.e: Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons.

items.q: Emma photographed these phases about 3.7 days apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: In a model, Noah walks a globe around a lamp. At each stop, he faces away from the lamp. What does facing away from the lamp show?
c: the night sky seen at midnight at that time of year
items.e: Midnight is when you face directly away from the sun.

items.q: At midnight, Pegasus is high in the sky. In which month is this?
items.e: In September, Earth's night side faces toward Pegasus.

items.q: Which tool would help Hana measure how far a star moves in an hour?
c: her fist held at arm's length (about 10°)
a ruler laid on the ground
items.e: A fist at arm's length covers about 10° of sky, a handy way to measure angles.

items.q: At midnight, Ethan is high in the sky. In which month is this?
items.e: In March, Earth's night side faces toward Ethan.

items.q: Why do shadows change direction during a sunny day?
c: The Sun appears to move across the sky as the Earth turns.
items.e: Link to the Earth's spin.

items.q: Why do more people see a lunar eclipse than a total solar eclipse?
c: Everyone on Earth's night side can see the shadowed Moon, but the Moon's shadow on Earth is small.
Lunar eclipses last only a second.
items.e: Earth's shadow is large.

items.q: Liam sees a first-quarter Moon. What fraction of the Moon's face looks lit?
items.e: “Quarter” means a quarter of the way through the cycle.

items.q: How could you model day and night in class?
c: Move the flashlight round a still globe.
Shine a flashlight on a globe and slowly turn the globe.
items.e: The Earth turns.

items.q: Why do astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises a day?
c: The Sun moves faster in space.
They orbit the Earth about 16 times a day.
items.e: Fast orbit.

items.q: Liam is high in the sky at midnight in March. Which constellation is high at midnight 9 months later?
items.e: 9 months later it is December, and the night side faces Orion.

items.q: Which model best explains a solar eclipse?
c: Sun → Earth → Moon in a straight line
Sun → Moon → Earth in a straight line
Earth → Sun → Moon in a straight line
items.e: The Moon's shadow hits Earth.

items.q: Ava models phases with a lamp (Sun), a ball (Moon) and her head (Earth). Where should the ball be to show a full moon?
c: between her head and the lamp
on the opposite side of her head from the lamp
items.e: Full moon: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.

items.q:
ConstellationBest month to see it in the evening
TaurusDecember
GeminiFebruary
ScorpiusJuly
AndromedaNovember
Which constellation is best seen on summer evenings?
items.e: Scorpius is best seen in July, which is in summer.

items.q: At midnight, Orion is high in the sky. In which month is this?
items.e: In December, Earth's night side faces toward Orion.

items.q: Ava sketches the Big Dipper at 8 p.m. and again at 11 p.m. What will her second sketch show?
c: The Big Dipper turned around Polaris.
The Big Dipper in exactly the same place.
items.e: The pattern keeps its shape but turns around Polaris as Earth spins.

items.q:
ConstellationBest month to see it in the evening
AndromedaNovember
TaurusDecember
OrionJanuary
CygnusAugust
Which constellation is best seen on fall evenings?
items.e: Andromeda is best seen in November, which is in fall.

items.q: Why were sundials used before clocks?
c: The Sun's shadow moves in a regular way as the Earth spins.
items.e: Regular motion.

items.q: Orion is high in the sky at midnight in December. Which constellation is high at midnight 9 months later?
items.e: 9 months later it is September, and the night side faces Pegasus.

items.q: Zoe's model shows Earth closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it still winter in Canada then?
c: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun.
items.e: Tilt matters more than distance.

items.q: Why do astronomers make star charts for each month?
c: Stars only shine in some months.
The stars visible in the evening change during the year.
The stars move to new places forever.
items.e: Monthly charts show which part of the sky is up in the evening.
